This report delivers a technical audit and statutory analysis of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework of Canada as of November 2026, written in Canadian English.

Canada's flagship innovation incentive—the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—underwent its most significant legislative expansion in decades with the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026. Applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and to depreciable property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024), the reformed statutory regime doubles the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), widens the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extends the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15,000,000–$75,000,000 three-year average gross revenue phase-out (which CCPCs may also elect to use under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)), and restores the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for both the income deduction pool and the ITC calculation. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process providing up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and halving the post-filing expenditure review service standard from 180 to 90 calendar days for claims with pre-approved projects.

At the sub-national level, provincial alignment with the federal Bill C-15 reforms has been uneven, requiring careful multi-jurisdictional modelling. British Columbia enacted Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026, making its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent and aligning with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, ECPC refundability, and capital expenditure restoration. Ontario retained its $3,000,000 expenditure limit ($240,000 maximum refund) and $25,000,000–$50,000,000 taxable capital / $500,000–$800,000 taxable income phase-outs for the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), and the Ontario Ministry of Finance's OITC program page continues to state that capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 are no longer qualified expenditures; the OITC operates alongside the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC). Québec replaced seven legacy innovation tax measures with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation—CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, providing a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital property and 50% of subcontractor costs) above an employee-indexed exclusion threshold (minimum $50,000), and 20% on the excess.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2024–2026 Statutory Overhaul
1.1 Statutory Foundations of the Federal SR&ED Program

Originally introduced in 1944, the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program operates as an entitlement-based tax incentive embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (the Act) and the Income Tax Regulations (the Regulations). Unlike discretionary government grants that are rationed by program budgets or competitive scoring, any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs qualifying SR&ED work and satisfies the statutory filing requirements is legally entitled to claim SR&ED tax incentives. According to practitioner guides, the program supports more than 24,160 businesses annually and is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance, issues policy guidelines, and processes claims.
The statutory architecture of the federal SR&ED regime rests on five interconnected pillars of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations:

items: Definition of Eligible Work (Subsection 248(1) of the Act): Defines "scientific research and experimental development" across basic research, applied research, experimental development, and eight enumerated categories of eligible support work, while carving out seven statutory exclusion paragraphs in paragraphs (e) through (k).

Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Section 37 of the Act): Subsection 37(1) establishes a running expenditure pool allowing taxpayers to deduct qualifying current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and restored capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) against business income in the year incurred or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in future taxation years. Subsections 37(8) and 37(10) govern the annual election between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method for computing SR&ED expenditures.

SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Section 127 of the Act): Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) against Part I tax otherwise payable, with unused credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward. Subsection 127(9) defines "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," "specified percentage" (15% basic rate), "contract payment," "government assistance," "non-government assistance," "first term shared-use-equipment," "second term shared-use-equipment," and "eligible Canadian public corporation". Subsections 127(10.1) through 127(10.8) govern the 20% enhancement (creating the enhanced 35% ITC rate), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, associated corporation sharing rules, and short taxation year prorations. Subsections 127(27) through 127(36) establish the 20-year ITC recapture mechanism upon disposition or commercial conversion of SR&ED property.

Refundable Investment Tax Credits (Section 127.1 of the Act): Subsections 127.1(1) and 127.1(2) govern the cash refundability of earned ITCs (at 100% or 40% refund rates) for Qualifying Corporations, other CCPCs, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, individuals, and certain trusts.

Regulatory Expenditure Mechanics (Part XXIX of the Regulations): Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations defines directly attributable current and overhead expenditures under the Traditional Method (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), sets the calculation and 55% rate of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method (subsection 2900(4)), establishes the All or Substantially All (ASA) proxy salary rule (subsection 2900(5)), imposes the overall PPA cap (subsection 2900(6)) and specified employee proxy restrictions (subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8)), lists salary base exclusions (subsection 2900(9)), and defines Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) excluded from shared-use equipment (subsection 2900(11)). Section 2902 defines prescribed expenditures that are excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and the CRA Eligibility Framework
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Statutory Structure

Whether scientific or technical activities qualify for Canadian R&D tax incentives is governed strictly by the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The statutory definition is structured as a three-tier legal filter: a mandatory methodological preamble and three core categories of research in paragraphs (a), (b), and (c); an exhaustive list of eight categories of eligible support work in paragraph (d); and seven statutory exclusion paragraphs in paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under the preamble to subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Within this framework, paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research aims to expand the fundamental scientific knowledge base and is conducted not only by universities and research institutes, but also by commercial enterprises in fields such as biotechnology, nanotechnology, advanced materials, and computer science. Paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, seeking to generate conceptual scientific understanding targeted at a practical commercial or medical objective (for example, investigating viral mechanisms to develop a novel vaccine). Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development) covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada, and the statute explicitly protects incremental improvements to existing materials, devices, products, or processes, provided those improvements require resolving genuine technological uncertainty to achieve a technological advancement.

In addition to core research and experimental development, paragraph 248(1)(d) (Eligible Support Work) encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight specific disciplines—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work does not constitute SR&ED on its own; its eligibility is derivative and requires both a direct functional nexus ("directly in support of") and proportionality in scope ("commensurate with the needs") to core basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada.
Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) stipulate that SR&ED does not include work with respect to any of the following excluded activities:

items: (e) market research or sales promotion;
(f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes;
(g) research in the social sciences or the humanities;
(h) prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas;
(i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
(j) style changes; or
(k) routine data collection.

body.text: In applying subsection 248(1), both the Tax Court of Canada and the CRA emphasize that the exclusions in paragraphs (e) to (k) are evaluated after core eligible work under paragraphs (a) to (c) has been identified, and that purpose distinguishes paragraph (d) support work from paragraphs (e)–(k) excluded work. For example, data collection or testing conducted for routine commercial quality assurance falls under the exclusions in paragraphs (f) and (k), whereas data collection or testing carried out specifically to test a scientific or technological hypothesis within an experimental development project qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d).
2.2 The CRA's Two-Pillar "Why" and "How" Guidelines vs. the Five-Question Judicial Test

Prior to August 2021, the CRA administered work eligibility under its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (issued in 2014/2015), which structured the technical review around the five sequential questions established by Justice Bowman in the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC):

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced its 2015 policy with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain binding judicial law in the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal (where all five questions must be answered in the affirmative, as reaffirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72), the CRA's 2021 Guidelines synthesize those five criteria into two overarching, cumulative requirements derived directly from the text of subsection 248(1): The "Why" Requirement and The "How" Requirement.
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement)

The "Why" requirement integrates Questions 1 and 4 of Northwest Hydraulic. Work must be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA defines advancement as the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge (such as explanatory theories, structural relationships, or predictive models) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely factual knowledge (such as routine measurements or performance metrics).

Crucially, new scientific or technological knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that it is unknown or uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in the scientific or technological knowledge available at the outset of the work. The baseline of available knowledge encompasses both publicly accessible scientific and engineering knowledge (standard practice, literature, vendor specifications) and the internal technical resources and expertise of the claimant's business environment. Under the CRA's Guidelines, seven specific technical indicators point to an insufficiency in available technological knowledge: (1) existing design methods or engineering rules are not applicable to the problem; (2) required specifications or performance targets do not conform to existing standards; (3) the system involves too many interacting variables or unknowns to predict behaviour; (4) operating parameters or environmental conditions fall outside normal operating ranges; (5) the nature of the technical problem is dynamically evolving as constraints interact; (6) essential behavioural or material data is not readily available; or (7) the design faces interlocking constraints (including economic or cost-target constraints that force a departure from known engineering solutions).

Three vital legal principles govern the "Why" requirement in audit and litigation practice. First, under the doctrine of system uncertainty, even where individual components or open-source software modules are commercially known, combining or integrating them in a novel architecture where their interactions cannot be predicted by a competent professional creates eligible system uncertainty (Northwest Hydraulic, 1998 TCC; Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18; Dazzm Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129; Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7). Second, if a business encounters a technological uncertainty but chooses to circumvent or sidestep it using a standard workaround based on existing knowledge rather than attempting to resolve the underlying uncertainty, the work does not meet the "Why" requirement; similarly, acquiring existing knowledge through employee training, hiring external consultants, or purchasing proprietary technology does not constitute attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Third, whether the project succeeds or fails in achieving its commercial or technical objective is legally irrelevant: as established in Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, [1999] 4 C.T.C. 2008 (TCC) and codified in the CRA Guidelines, conclusively disproving a scientific or technological hypothesis generates new knowledge by eliminating a potential pathway and therefore constitutes a valid technological advancement.
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search by Experiment or Analysis)

The "How" requirement integrates Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic. Merely working in an organized, professional, or methodical manner (or engaging in trial-and-error prototyping without formulating causal hypotheses) does not constitute a "systematic investigation or search". To satisfy the "How" requirement, the claimant must demonstrate four sequential steps:

items: Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating an idea consistent with known scientific or technological facts that serves as a starting point for investigation toward resolving the uncertainty (expressed as a proposed causal mechanism, mathematical model, or technical approach).

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Subjecting the hypothesis to rigorous physical experimentation, prototyping tests, or mathematical/computational simulation and analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively as results are observed.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Analysing the quantitative or qualitative test results against the hypothesis to draw logical conclusions regarding why the tested approach succeeded or failed.
Maintaining Contemporaneous Evidence: Keeping dated records, test logs, commit histories, data sets, photographs, or prototypes generated as the work progresses.

body.text: 3. Federal SR&ED Two-Pronged Incentive Mechanics: Deduction Pool and Investment Tax Credits

The federal SR&ED program delivers two distinct financial benefits that operate sequentially: (1) a 100% tax deduction via the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the Act, and (2) an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) of 15% or 35% under sections 127 and 127.1 of the Act.
3.1 The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Subsection 37(1))

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada are accumulated in a dedicated tax pool rather than being deducted under general income computation rules in section 9 or depreciated under Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules in paragraph 20(1)(a). Calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661 (Lines 429 to 470), the subsection 37(1) pool aggregates both current and restored capital expenditures.

On the additions side of the ledger, paragraph 37(1)(a) adds 100% of allowable current expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), 100% of payments for SR&ED performed on behalf of the taxpayer by arm's length or non-arm's length contractors (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), and 100% of eligible third-party payments to corporations (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)), approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)), or tax-exempt paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit R&D corporations (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)). Note that while arm's length contracts and third-party payments are restricted to 80% for ITC purposes, 100% of those expenditures enter the subsection 37(1) deductible pool. Following the enactment of Bill C-15, paragraph 37(1)(b) also adds 100% of eligible capital expenditures made to acquire new or used depreciable property that became available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, and that meets the All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) operating time or consumed-value test (Line 390 of Form T661). Any amount deducted from the pool in respect of capital property is deemed by subsection 37(6) to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed for the property. Additional pool additions include repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (Line 445), any undeducted pool balance carried forward from the preceding taxation year (Line 450), pool balances inherited upon an amalgamation (subsection 87(2)) or wind-up (subsection 88(1)) (Line 452), and any SR&ED ITC recaptured into Part I tax in the immediately preceding taxation year (Line 453).

On the reductions side of the ledger, paragraph 37(1)(d) requires subtracting provincial/territorial R&D tax credits (unless timely renounced) (Line 429), other government grants or subsidies (Line 431), and non-government assistance (Line 432) received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received in the year in respect of claimed SR&ED expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit attributable to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool (because the PPA is never in the pool); instead, that portion is included directly in taxable income on Schedule T2SCH1. Furthermore, under paragraph 37(1)(e) (Line 435), any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax payable, carried back to prior years, or received as a cash refund in the preceding taxation year reduces the current year's subsection 37(1) pool, preventing a double benefit of both a tax credit and an income deduction on the same dollar. Finally, when depreciable SR&ED capital property that was included in the pool is sold or disposed of, the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted pool balance for the property reduces the pool on Line 440 (with any excess proceeds up to original capital cost included in income as CCA recapture on Schedule T2SCH1).

A corporation or individual may deduct any amount from the available pool (Line 455) in the current taxation year (Line 460) and carry the remaining balance (Line 470) forward indefinitely to future taxation years. Unlike non-capital losses (which expire after 20 years), the subsection 37(1) pool never expires (subject to acquisition-of-control streaming rules), allowing taxpayers to preserve the pool during loss years or low-tax-rate years. By contrast, partnerships are subject to three strict statutory exceptions under paragraphs 96(1)(e.1) and 96(1)(g), subsection 127(12.1), and the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy: (1) a partnership must deduct 100% of its available subsection 37(1) pool in the fiscal period incurred and cannot carry forward any pool balance to future years; (2) under subsection 127(12.1), any SR&ED ITC allocated to partners reduces the partnership's subsection 37(1) pool in the same fiscal period (rather than the following year), regardless of whether the partners actually claim the ITC; and (3) under paragraph 96(1)(g), a limited partner (or specified member) cannot deduct any portion of a partnership business loss that was created or increased by the partnership's SR&ED pool deduction.
3.2 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Caps, and Refundability Rules (Sections 127 and 127.1)

The second and primary financial incentive is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC), calculated on Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570 of Form T661) and claimed on Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit — Corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)).

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (revised October 7, 2026 to incorporate the enacted Bill C-15 rules), the ITC rate (35% enhanced vs. 15% basic) and the cash refundability rate (100%, 40%, or 0%) depend on the legal classification of the claimant, whether the expenditure is within or above the claimant's annual expenditure limit, and whether the expenditure is of a current or capital nature. body.text: Several critical statutory nuances in this matrix govern corporate tax planning. First, although Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 to earn the enhanced 35% ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit for CCPCs and ECPCs, the cash refund rate under section 127.1 on the unclaimed balance of ITCs earned on capital expenditures is 40% (producing an immediate cash refund of 35% × 40% = 14% of the capital cost, with the remaining 21% ITC available to offset Part I tax payable or carry back 3 years / carry forward 20 years), whereas the cash refund rate on current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) up to the expenditure limit is 100% (producing a full 35% cash refund). Second, all CCPCs (other than excluded corporations) whose prior-year taxable capital is below the $75,000,000 upper phase-out limit earn the 35% ITC with 100% refundability on current expenditures up to their expenditure limit, even if their prior-year taxable income exceeded the Qualifying Income Limit ("CCPCs other than Qualifying or Excluded Corporations"). However, to earn a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC for expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the CCPC must meet the definition of a "Qualifying Corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)—meaning its taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) for the preceding taxation year did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. Third, under subsection 127(8) of the Act, a partnership cannot be a CCPC or ECPC, and therefore SR&ED ITCs earned through a partnership are calculated at the 15% basic rate and allocated to the partners; as established in All Colour Chemicals Ltd. v. The Queen (1993 TCC), a CCPC that conducts SR&ED as a partner in a partnership forfeits the 35% enhanced rate on partnership expenditures.
3.3 Expenditure Limit and Qualifying Income Limit Formulas
1. CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit for a CCPC (and its associated CCPCs) was $3,000,000, phasing out linearly as the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (TC, as defined for former Part I.3 Tax on Large Corporations) increased from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000:

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 increased the base expenditure limit to $6,000,000 and expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out span, where every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the expenditure limit by $1):

Once the prior-year taxable capital of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) reaches $75,000,000, the expenditure limit becomes nil ($0), and all qualified expenditures earn only the 15% non-refundable basic ITC.
2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) & Revenue-Based Phase-Out (Subsections 127(9), 127(10.6), 127(10.31) and 127(10.32))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—defined in subsection 127(9) for Canadian-resident public corporations not controlled by non-residents—qualifies for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

Rather than using taxable capital, an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out linearly based on its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (R), determined from the financial statements of the corporation (or the consolidated financial statements of its consolidated group, with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales) over the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range:

Furthermore, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the Act, a CCPC that is not associated with another corporation (subsection 127(10.31)) or a group of associated CCPCs (subsection 127(10.32)) may file a prescribed election to calculate its expenditure limit using this three-year average gross revenue formula instead of prior-year taxable capital. This election is particularly advantageous for capital-intensive biotechnology, hardware, cleantech, or deep-tech CCPCs that have raised substantial debt or equity capital exceeding $15,000,000 (which inflates taxable capital employed in Canada) while still remaining pre-revenue or generating less than $15,000,000 in three-year average gross revenue.
3. Qualifying Income Limit Formula (Subsection 127.1(2))

To determine whether a CCPC qualifies as a "Qualifying Corporation" (entitling it to a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the expenditure limit), its prior-year taxable income (combined with associated corporations) must not exceed the Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the formula under subsection 127.1(2) is updated to match the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out span:
Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) / $60,000,000]

where A is nil ($0) if prior-year taxable capital is ≤ $15,000,000, and otherwise equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula used $40,000,000 in place of $60,000,000 and a $10,000,000 threshold for A).
4. Short Taxation Years and Associated Group Allocations

If a corporation has a short taxation year (less than 51 weeks), its expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the otherwise determined expenditure limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365. Associated CCPCs must share the single $6,000,000 expenditure limit by filing Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3), and under subsection 127(10.5), special proration rules apply when an associated CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year.
4. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Methodological Elections
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subsections 37(8) and 37(10); Regulation 2900)

Under subsection 37(8) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a claimant must choose each taxation year between two mutually exclusive methodologies for computing SR&ED expenditures and overhead: the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)). The election is made in Part 3, Section A of Form T661 (Line 160 for the Proxy Method; Line 162 for the Traditional Method) when the claim for the taxation year is first filed. Pursuant to subsection 37(10) of the Act, if no election is made, the Traditional Method applies by default, and once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is legally irrevocable for that year.

Under the Proxy Method, instead of tracking, substantiating, and claiming actual SR&ED overhead and other indirect expenditures on Line 360, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount called the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661. Pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, since the 2014 calendar year, the PPA is equal to 55% of the salary base (reduced from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013). The salary base (Line 818 of Form T661) consists solely of the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (and permissible outside-Canada salaries), excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, unpaid remuneration from prior years (Line 310), and subject to strict caps for specified employees (Regulations 2900(7) to 2900(9)) and an overall PPA cap based on total business expenses (Regulation 2900(6)).

Crucially, the PPA (Line 502 of Form T661) is included in Qualified SR&ED Expenditures to earn the 15% or 35% SR&ED ITC, but is never included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9(1) of the Act.

body.text: 4.2 Detailed Rules for Each Qualifying Expenditure Category
1. Salaries and Wages (SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, Updated January 28, 2025)

Under subsection 248(1) and section 5 of the Act, "salary or wages" means employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (gross T4 employment remuneration), including regular salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, cash outlays for taxable benefits, and bonuses/profit-based remuneration for non-specified employees, while excluding the employer's share of payroll benefits, extended vacation/sick leave, stock option benefits under section 7, and retiring allowances. To be claimed, the salary or wages must be incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada (or permissible outside-Canada work) and paid within the taxation year or within 180 days of the taxation year-end (subsection 78(4)).

Under the Proxy Method, only employees directly engaged in SR&ED may be claimed. "Directly engaged" means hands-on scientific or technical work (preparing equipment/materials for tests, running experiments, collecting experimental data, writing experimental code, mathematical modelling) as well as first-line technical supervision that directly steers the course of ongoing SR&ED. Non-technological management, executive oversight above the first-line supervisor, and clerical/administrative support (HR, accounting, payroll, purchasing, legal, maintenance) are not directly engaged. Under the Traditional Method, however, clerical and administrative staff salaries that directly aid ongoing SR&ED and satisfy the incremental test can be claimed as overhead on Line 360. Under Regulation 2900(5) and Section 7.3.4 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an employee spends 90% or more (ASA) of their total working time during the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages for the year is deemed to be for SR&ED; otherwise, only the exact reasonable proportion of time spent on SR&ED is eligible.

Strict statutory limits apply to "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a specified shareholder owning directly or indirectly 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. First, for the expenditure pool and direct wage lines (Lines 305 and 309), a specified employee's claimable SR&ED salary excludes all bonuses and remuneration based on profits (subsection 37(9)) and is capped under subsection 37(9.1) at 5 × the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the tax year on which the individual is a specified employee (and shared among associated corporations via Form T1174 under subsection 37(9.3)). Based on official CRA YMPE announcements—$71,300 for 2025, $74,600 for 2026, and $76,700 for 2027 (announced October 28, 2026)—the maximum annual 5 × YMPE direct SR&ED salary cap for a specified employee is $356,500 for 2025, $373,000 for 2026, and $383,500 for 2027. Second, when calculating the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 (Boxes 850–860) under Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8), the amount included for each specified employee is further restricted to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total base salary or wages for the year (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit remuneration, taxable benefits, and Line 310 prior-year unpaid wages) (Box 856), and (b) 2.5 × YMPE × (days employed in the tax year ÷ 365) (Box 858). For a full 365-day year, the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base cap is $178,250 for 2025, $186,500 for 2026, and $191,750 for 2027.

Under subsection 78(4) of the Act (Lines 310 and 315), any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and are instead deemed incurred in the subsequent taxation year when paid (reported on Line 315 in the year accrued and claimed on Line 310 when paid, though Line 310 amounts are excluded from the Part 5 PPA salary base). Finally, under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) (Lines 307 and 309), permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed physically outside Canada may be claimed up to a maximum cap of 10% of total in-Canada SR&ED salaries and wages (10% of [Line 300 + Line 305]), provided the work is performed directly by an employee (never a contractor) who was a resident of Canada when the expense was incurred, the work is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant, and the remuneration is not subject to an income or profits tax of another country.
2. Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" means physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or component items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible object on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Materials may be purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided they are consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada, and their cost is claimable only in the taxation year in which actual consumption or transformation occurs (not when held in inventory).

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (or whose scrap value is less than 10% of total cost). Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom product, experimental production run, or commercial asset that retains value after the SR&ED concludes. While 100% of the cost of materials transformed is claimable in the year of transformation, any subsequent sale of the resulting product or conversion of the asset to commercial use within 20 taxation years triggers SR&ED ITC Recapture under subsection 127(27). Items that do not compose the physical body of the thing on which SR&ED is performed—such as beakers, petri dishes, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, lubricants, CDs/DVDs, and general utilities (electricity, water, natural gas)—do not qualify as materials consumed or transformed; they are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method or claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method.
3. Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's length taxable supplier (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01); Line 340) to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool, and 80% qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (20% is deducted on Line 529 pursuant to subsection 127(9)). Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (revised March 30, 2022), a payer may also claim an arm's length contract that consists solely of paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, provided that support work is directly in support of, and commensurate with the needs of, core basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada by or on behalf of the payer. Under the Capital Look-Through Rule (subsections 37(14) and 37(15)), any portion of a contract payment that relates to non-current (capital) expenditures of the performer must be excluded, and the performer is legally required to notify the payer in writing of that reduction within 90 days of calendar year-end.

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (section 251; Line 345), the payer may include the expenditure in its subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but paragraph 127(9)(f) and subsection 127(24) exclude the NAL contract payment from the payer's Qualified Expenditures (meaning the payer earns 0% ITC directly). Instead, the NAL performer's receipts are not treated as a contract payment, allowing the NAL performer to claim the SR&ED ITC on its own underlying expenditures (and under subsection 37(13), support work performed by a NAL performer is deemed SR&ED to the extent linked to the payer's core SR&ED). Alternatively, the NAL performer and payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer up to 100% of the performer's qualified expenditures (Line 540/544 for the transferor; Line 508 for the transferee) to the payer (if the performer attempts to transfer an amount exceeding its actual qualified expenditure pool at year-end, no amount can be transferred). Furthermore, when a claimant purchases goods or non-SR&ED services from a NAL supplier for use in SR&ED, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the actual cost to the NAL supplier (Lines 541–542).

Under the Third-Party Payments Policy (updated January 26, 2026) and subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) (Line 370), payments made to approved associations, approved universities, colleges, research institutes, granting councils, or tax-exempt paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant's business—where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED—qualify as third-party payments. Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool and 80% eligible for the SR&ED ITC (less 20% on Line 529), and require filing a separate Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).
4. Overhead, Cloud Computing, Software Licences, and Prescribed Exclusions

Under the Traditional Method, overhead and other current expenditures can be claimed on Line 360 only if they satisfy two cumulative regulatory tests under Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3) and the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy: (1) the Directly Related Test (requiring a direct, unmediated link between the expenditure and the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used in SR&ED), and (2) the Incremental Test (requiring that the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred). Fixed monthly base charges for office internet or telephone lines fail the incremental test, whereas metered long-distance or dedicated data transmission charges incurred specifically for SR&ED testing qualify.

With respect to cloud computing and software licences, under the Proxy Method, cloud computing expenses and SaaS software subscriptions are not physical materials and cannot be claimed separately on Form T661; they are treated as overhead covered notionally by the 55% PPA and deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9(1). Under the Traditional Method, metered cloud compute costs and single-year software development tool licences used strictly in SR&ED can be claimed as overhead on Line 360 to the extent they are directly related and incremental to the SR&ED project. Furthermore, under Section 10.0 of the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), computer software and systems software licences with an enduring useful life exceeding one year (prescribed CCA classes) acquired after December 15, 2024 qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures on Line 390 if acquired strictly as an SR&ED tool (e.g., computer-aided design software used ASA ≥90% in SR&ED), whereas software intended to be incorporated into a commercial product is strictly excluded.

Finally, even if an expenditure is incremental to SR&ED under the Traditional Method, section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations designates specific outlays as prescribed expenditures (Line 530) that cannot be included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes: fees paid for preparing financial or technical portions of SR&ED claims; costs to attend conventions or conferences; dues or fees for membership in scientific or technical societies; legal or accounting fees; interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g); entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses; fines or penalties; and expenditures for used or refurbished depreciable capital property (paragraph 2902(b)). Recruitment expenses (headhunter fees, job advertising, candidate interview travel, and immigration/work permit fees) are likewise deductible only as regular business expenses and do not qualify for the SR&ED pool or ITCs.
4.3 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from the federal SR&ED program. Bill C-15 restored capital and lease expenditure eligibility for property acquired (and available for use) and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, governed by three updated CRA policies: the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), and the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026).
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures — All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) (Line 390)

To claim 100% of the capital cost of depreciable property on Line 390 of Form T661 (and report the 10 most expensive properties per project on Lines 262–263 and Boxes 782 and 786), the property must satisfy five cumulative criteria:

items: Post-December 15, 2024 Acquisition & Available-for-Use Rule: The property must be acquired after December 15, 2024, and pursuant to subsections 13(27) and 37(1.2) of the Act, can only be claimed in the taxation year in which it becomes available for use.

Depreciable Property Owned by Claimant: Must be depreciable property (for which CCA would otherwise be allowed under Part XI of the Regulations) owned by the claimant. Land (non-depreciable) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (except prescribed special-purpose SR&ED buildings) are strictly excluded. Under the Proxy Method, General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, filing cabinets, photocopiers, standard office telephones) is also excluded, whereas specialized servers, GPU compute infrastructure, lab apparatus, testing rigs, and dedicated R&D computers qualify.

Intent Test at Acquisition (ASA ≥90% Operating Time or Consumed Value): At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend (substantiated by business plans, capital budgets, project proposals, and equipment logbooks) that the property will either be used All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time over its entire expected useful life for SR&ED carried on in Canada, or have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (such as rapid technological obsolescence or physical destruction during testing, in which case the length of the SR&ED project relative to normal useful life is irrelevant).

New vs. Used Equipment: Both new and used depreciable property meeting the ASA test are included on Line 390 and added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool; however, used or refurbished equipment is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the Regulations and must be deducted on Line 530, earning 0% ITC.

body.text: 2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) — Primarily (>50% to <90%) Used in SR&ED (Line 504 & Part 6C)

When new machinery, hardware, or lab equipment is used in both SR&ED and commercial operations such that it does not meet the ≥90% lifetime intent test, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) of the Act and the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026). To qualify, the asset must be new depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, must not be GPOEF, and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes property intended at acquisition to be used during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility or plant and intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life).

Unlike ASA capital property (which is tested on lifetime intent), SUE is tested on actual operating time (primarily = more than 50% and less than 90% of total operating hours) across two statutory periods. For First-Term SUE, the First Period begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that date. If actual SR&ED use exceeds 50% of operating time during the First Period, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowing costs under section 21 and adjusted for NAL rules under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies on Line 504 to earn the 35% or 15% ITC. For Second-Term SUE, the Second Period begins when the property was acquired and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that date. Provided the asset qualified as First-Term SUE and its cumulative actual SR&ED operating time across the Second Period exceeds 50%, a second 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies on Line 504 to earn the 35% or 15% ITC (bringing total qualified expenditures across both terms to 50% of the capital cost). The capital cost of SUE does not enter the subsection 37(1) SR&ED pool; instead, the asset is depreciated under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the following taxation year under subsection 13(7.1). Claimants must report the 20 most expensive SUE properties in Part 6C of Form T661 (Boxes 788, 790, 792, 794, and 796).
3. Equipment Lease Costs (Lines 350 and 360)
Lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify under two pathways (lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024 remain ineligible):

items: Used ASA (≥90% of Operating Time) in SR&ED (Line 350): Claimable under both the Traditional and Proxy methods on Line 350 (except lease costs for GPOEF, which are excluded under the Proxy Method).

Used Less Than 90% of Operating Time in SR&ED (Line 360): Claimable only under the Traditional Method on Line 360 as overhead to the extent the lease cost is directly related and incremental to the SR&ED (allocated by the percentage of SR&ED operating time).

body.text: 4.4 The 20-Year SR&ED ITC Recapture Regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a taxpayer earns an SR&ED ITC on a property (including materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, or physical property acquired via an SR&ED contract) and, within 20 taxation years of acquiring the property (subsection 127(36)), disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the previously earned ITC is recaptured and added directly to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion.

For ASA capital property or materials transformed, the recapture equals the lesser of: (a) the exact ITC previously earned on the property, and (b) the "specified percentage" (the ITC rate—35% or 15%—at which the credit was originally earned) multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property at the time of commercial conversion or non-arm's length disposition. For Shared-Use Equipment, the proceeds of disposition or FMV are scaled by 25% (if only First-Term SUE was claimed) or 50% (if both First-Term and Second-Term SUE were claimed) before multiplying by the ITC rate.

As illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant manufactures an experimental prototype in-house using $4,000 of SR&ED wages, $1,000 of overhead, and $5,000 of purchased materials transformed, only the $5,000 cost of materials transformed is subject to recapture upon commercial conversion; in-house SR&ED salaries and overhead are never subject to recapture. By contrast, if the claimant paid an arm's length supplier $12,000 under a contract to build the component, the entire $12,000 contract cost of the physical property is subject to recapture. However, under the de minimis scrap sale exemption, if an experimental product or prototype is sold as scrap for proceeds of disposition that are less than 10% of the total cost (labour, overhead, and materials combined) to produce it, the CRA applies no ITC recapture. Any federal SR&ED ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the claimant's subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year (Line 453 of Form T661).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Post-Bill C-15 Alignment

Every Canadian province except Prince Edward Island (alongside the Yukon Territory, while the Northwest Territories and Nunavut do not offer R&D tax credits) provides a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that stacks on top of the federal SR&ED program. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces both the federal subsection 37(1) expenditure pool (Line 429) and federal qualified expenditures (Lines 513–514) unless the claimant validly renounces/waives a non-refundable provincial credit on or before its filing due date.

body.text: 5.1 Deep-Dive Analysis of Major Provincial Regimes
1. Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario operates a three-tier corporate R&D tax credit system under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered by the CRA through the T2 return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96; Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000). Unlike the federal enhanced credit, OITC eligibility is not restricted strictly to CCPCs (any non-exempt corporation under the phase-out thresholds can qualify), but Ontario did not increase its $3,000,000 expenditure limit to match the federal $6,000,000 cap. Furthermore, the $3,000,000 OITC limit phases out linearly if prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or if prior-year Ontario specified paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Notably, the Ontario Ministry of Finance's OITC program page has not been updated to reflect the federal restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and continues to state that capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 are no longer qualified expenditures, so claimants should confirm the Ontario treatment of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures before including them on Schedule 566 or Schedule 508.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45; Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (with no expenditure cap). Because the OITC is treated as government assistance for ORDTC purposes, the eligible expenditure base for the 3.5% ORDTC is reduced by any 8% OITC claimed (meaning that on the first $3,000,000 of expenditures where OITC is claimed, the effective ORDTC rate is 3.5% × (1 − 0.08) = 3.22%). Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, or a corporation in a tax-loss position may deliver a written waiver on or before 6 months after its tax year-end to waive the ORDTC so that the unutilized non-refundable credit does not reduce its 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC. If property on which ORDTC was claimed is sold or converted to commercial use, Ontario applies a grossed-up recapture rate of 23.56% to the recaptured credit. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97; Schedules 568 and 569) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on current SR&ED expenditures paid in money under an eligible contract with an unconnected eligible Ontario research institute (Ontario universities, community colleges, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence) where the corporation is entitled to exploit the results, up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (maximum annual refund of $4,000,000), and small businesses can stack both the 20% OBRITC and the 8% OITC on the same eligible contract.
2. Québec: The CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) and the IDCI IP Box

In its 2025–2026 Budget, the Gouvernement du Québec enacted a sweeping restructuring of its provincial innovation tax regime, replacing seven separate tax measures—including the legacy R&D salary tax credit (Form RD-1029.7, which provided 14% to 30% on wages), the university/public research centre credit (Form RD-1029.8.6.1), the private partnership pre-competitive research credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the research consortium credit, the technological adaptation services credit, the industrial design tax credit, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts—with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC) for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025.

While Québec's definition of R&D remains harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) (and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of the R&D portion), the CRIC adds two major expansions administered by Revenu Québec. First, eligible pre-commercialization activities cover regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies aimed at obtaining initial certification or regulatory approval, as well as product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, choice of materials, and initial certification quality control systems), provided the pre-commercialization work is carried out in Québec in conjunction with and as a continuation of R&D performed in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Second, capital property acquisition costs are eligible at 100% for depreciable capital assets used in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec (excluding land, buildings, and rights to use land/buildings, and provided the property is not claimed under the C3i investment tax credit or a large investment project tax holiday). Under the CRIC, qualified Québec expenditures comprise: 100% of salaries and wages of employees engaged in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for work carried out in Québec; 50% of payments to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of eligible capital property acquisition costs (Québec does not use the federal 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount).

Before the CRIC applies, total qualified expenditures in the taxation year must exceed the applicable exclusion threshold, which equals the greater of: (1) $50,000 (prorated for the number of days in a short taxation year), or (2) the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 for 2025) for each employee for whom the CRIC is claimed, multiplied by the percentage of time that employee devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the year. On qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, the corporation earns a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of excess expenditures—regardless of the corporation's total assets or whether it is a CCPC, public corporation, or foreign-controlled subsidiary (except for corporate members of a partnership, to which the 30% enhanced rate does not apply)—and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all qualified expenditures above the $1,000,000 cap. Claims are filed with the CO-17 return within 18 months of tax year-end using Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (plus RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated group allocation of the $1M limit, RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization project narratives, and Form RD-222 for the Québec R&D pool deduction), reported under Code 112 (R&D) and Code 113 (pre-commercialization).

Alongside the CRIC, while the federal government's patent box consultation (which closed April 15, 2024) has not yet resulted in federal legislation as of November 2026, Québec operates Canada's premier IP box regime: the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI). For taxation years beginning after December 31, 2020 (with a direct Québec R&D nexus required for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2023), the IDCI allows a qualified corporation with a Québec establishment to reduce its Québec corporate income tax rate on qualifying commercialization income attributable to a Qualified Intellectual Property Asset (QIPA)—including issued patents or pending patent applications (with a post-March 17, 2016 filing date), certificates of supplementary protection, copyright-protected software programs (created after March 10, 2020), and plant breeder's rights—from the general rate of 11.5% down to an effective rate of 2.0%.
6. Stacking Mechanics, Government Assistance, and Direct Grant Integration
6.1 Statutory Assistance Rules (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18) to 127(20))

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, investment allowances, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits) and non-government assistance (amounts includable under paragraph 12(1)(x) such as commercial inducements or reimbursements) reduce both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (paragraph 37(1)(d)) and qualified SR&ED expenditures (subsections 127(18) to 127(20)).
Four critical compliance rules govern assistance and grant stacking:

items: Accrual Recognition ("Received, Entitled to Receive, or Reasonably Expected to Receive"): Assistance must be deducted in the taxation year in which the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive the amount on or before the filing due date for the return (e.g., 6 months after corporate year-end), even if the cash grant or provincial tax refund is disbursed in a later year.

Project-by-Project Application and Carryforward (Subsections 127(18) and 127(19)): Reductions to qualified expenditures for assistance and contract payments are applied strictly on a project-by-project basis. Assistance received for Project A does not reduce the qualified expenditures of Project B; however, if assistance for Project A exceeds Project A's qualified expenditures in Year 1, the unapplied excess carries forward under subsection 127(19) to reduce Project A's qualified expenditures in subsequent taxation years. Furthermore, if a funding agreement fails to segregate SR&ED costs from non-SR&ED costs, the entire grant received in respect of the project reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Allocation Between Non-Arm's Length Parties (Subsection 127(20); Form T1145): When assistance is received by a group of non-arm's length parties, they may file Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to allocate the assistance reduction among the entities.

Repayment of Assistance (Subsection 127(10.7); Lines 445 and 560): When a conditional or repayable government contribution (such as an interest-free repayable contribution from a Regional Development Agency or the Strategic Innovation / Response Fund) is subsequently repaid, the repayment is added back to the subsection 37(1) pool on Line 445 and earns an SR&ED ITC on Line 560 at the exact ITC rate (35% or 15%) that applied in the year the assistance originally reduced the claim.

6.3 Stacking SR&ED with NRC IRAP and Other Federal Innovation Programs

A critical planning advantage under Canadian tax law arises when stacking the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) with the federal SR&ED Proxy Method. NRC IRAP provides non-repayable cost-shared R&D contributions (with NRC service standards covering contribution decisions from under $50,000 up to a $10,000,000 ceiling, and grant catalogue analyses reporting a median award of $75,000) that reimburse a negotiated percentage (frequently up to 80%) of direct R&D technical salaries.

When an NRC IRAP grant is received for an SR&ED project, the grant is deducted as Other Government Assistance on Line 431 (pool) and Line 515 (qualified expenditures) of Form T661. Crucially, under Part 5 of Form T661 and Regulation 2900(4), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base (Line 810/818) is NOT reduced by the NRC IRAP grant. Consequently, if a qualifying CCPC incurs $100,000 of direct R&D salary and receives a $60,000 (60%) NRC IRAP salary reimbursement:

items: The corporation still calculates its 55% PPA on the full $100,000 salary, generating $55,000 of PPA.
Gross Qualified Expenditures equal $100,000 salary + $55,000 PPA = $155,000.
Subtracting the $60,000 IRAP grant on Line 515 leaves $95,000 of net federal Qualified Expenditures.

At the 35% enhanced CCPC rate (before provincial credits), the corporation earns $33,250 in federal SR&ED cash refunds on top of the $60,000 IRAP grant, recovering $93,250 (93.25%) of its $100,000 salary outlay (and over 96% when stacked with provincial refundable credits).

body.text: Other major federal and co-funded innovation programs that interact with SR&ED include the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) / Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (for large-scale industrial projects with contributions from $10,000,000+, where non-repayable or concessional assistance reduces the SR&ED pool and qualified expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), as confirmed in CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC), and the Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits (Clean Technology ITC [up to 30%], Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC [30%], and CCUS ITC [37.5% to 60%]) enacted and expanded through Bill C-15. Taxpayers cannot claim both a Clean Economy ITC and the restored SR&ED capital ITC on the exact same dollar of capital property cost, requiring asset-by-asset segregation between commercial production lines (Clean Tech Manufacturing ITC) and dedicated R&D pilot/testing apparatus (SR&ED ITC).
7. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Prescribed Forms, and Part 9 Penalties
7.1 The Absolute 18-Month SR&ED Reporting Deadline and Subsection 220(2.2)

To access either the subsection 37(1) expenditure deduction or the subsection 127(5) / 127.1(1) Investment Tax Credit, a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before its statutory SR&ED reporting deadline. Subsection 37(11) of the Act governs the filing deadline for identifying expenditures on Form T661 to enter the subsection 37(1) pool, and paragraph 127(9)(m) governs the filing deadline for claiming ITCs on Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts). Both provisions set the SR&ED reporting deadline at 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred:

items: Corporations (T2 Corporation Income Tax Return): Standard T2 filing due date is 6 months after the corporate taxation year-end. Adding 12 months yields an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (e.g., for a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end, the T2 is due June 30, 2025, and the absolute SR&ED reporting deadline is June 30, 2026).

Individuals Carrying on a Business (T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return): Standard T1 filing due date is June 15 of the following calendar year. Adding 12 months yields an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 15 of the second following year (17.5 months after the December 31 tax year-end).

Trusts (T3 Trust Income Tax and Information Return): Standard T3 filing due date is 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end. Adding 12 months yields an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of 90 days plus 12 months after the trust's taxation year-end.

Partnerships (T5013 Partnership Information Return): Each partner's SR&ED reporting deadline is based on that partner's own tax year-end; to ensure all partners can claim their allocated ITCs, the partnership's Form T661 should be filed on or before the earliest partner's SR&ED reporting deadline.

body.text: If Form T661 is filed on or before the 18-month deadline, but Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) is omitted or filed after the 18-month deadline, the claimant may include the allowable expenditures in its subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but permanently forfeits 100% of the SR&ED ITC (Easyway Cattle Co. Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211). Conversely, if Form T661 is omitted or filed after the 18-month deadline, the expenditures are deemed never to be SR&ED expenditures, resulting in the permanent forfeiture of both the subsection 37(1) pool deduction and the SR&ED ITC. Pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act (applicable on and after November 17, 2005), a request to waive or extend filing requirements under subsection 220(2.1) cannot be made in respect of prescribed SR&ED forms or prescribed information. Because the CRA does not accept changes or modifications to a claim after the SR&ED reporting deadline has passed, the CRA recommends submitting the claim at least 90 days before the reporting deadline (i.e., within 15 months of corporate year-end) so the CRA has time to advise of any missing information prior to the statutory bar.
