body.text: To enhance predictability prior to filing, the CRA has offered three distinct advisory and pre-approval mechanisms, two of which remain available. First, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, allowing eligible businesses to obtain an up-front determination from the CRA on whether their planned or recently started R&D project qualifies as SR&ED before incurring significant costs. To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the applicant must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, be in good standing with the CRA, and submit a project that has not been included in a previous SR&ED claim and does not involve issues currently under litigation. The business requests a case number, completes the application and supporting documents, and uploads it via My Business Account, receiving a Pre-Claim Approval determination within 8 weeks. When filing Form T661, the claimant ticks Line 212 and enters the Pre-Claim Approval case number on Line 214. Second, the Pre-Claim Consultation service (launched September 27, 2023 to replace the legacy Pre-Claim Project Review and Account Executive services), which offered virtual consultations on up to 3 projects per tax year to help potential claimants determine whether there was SR&ED work in their projects before filing, is no longer available as of January 1, 2026. Third, the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) is a mandatory virtual educational session for selected claimants who are filing their first SR&ED claim or have not filed a claim in the preceding 3 taxation years; FTCAS is not an audit (any expected refund is processed after the meeting), and provides a written report with tailored recommendations on documentation and expenditure tracking for future claims.
8.2 CRA Processing Service Standards and the Three-Step Audit Review Process

Under the CRA's updated post-claim service standards (as of October 14, 2026), processing timelines apply strictly to refundable SR&ED claims (there are no service standards for non-refundable claims), with the CRA committed to meeting these standards 90% of the time:

items: Within 60 Calendar Days: Claims that are Accepted as Filed (AAF) without further review.
Within 90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for review that only include projects previously granted Pre-Claim Approval (cutting standard review time in half).

Within 180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for a full technical and/or financial review (including claims with unapproved projects or projects that materially diverged from their Pre-Claim Approval).

body.text: When a claim is selected for review (via automated AI/risk-assessment scoring or random sampling), the claim cannot be withdrawn. Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), the review is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates whether the work meets subsection 248(1)) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who evaluates whether claimed expenditures comply with sections 37 and 127 and Regulation 2900) across three formal steps.

In Step 1 (Start of the Review), the reviewer initiates contact by telephone to identify the projects and specific issues selected for review, confirm the participants, and schedule a virtual (or, exceptionally, on-site) review meeting. The CRA follows up with an Initial Letter summarizing the call, providing a meeting agenda, listing any pre-meeting document requests (subject to a standard 30-day response timeline), and supplying contact details for the RTA, FR, and their respective managers (Research and Technology Manager [RTM] and Financial Review Manager [FRM]). In Step 2 (The Review Meeting and Evidence Examination), the RTA and FR interview the personnel who directly performed or supervised the SR&ED work (noting that oral statements during interviews do not replace the requirement to maintain adequate written documentation), conduct a virtual or physical tour of the facilities, and examine the contemporaneous supporting evidence identified on Lines 270 to 282 of Form T661 (test logs, source code commit histories, engineering notebooks, failed prototypes, time sheets, T4s, general ledgers, and contracts). In Step 3 (Review Findings and the SR&ED Review Report), the RTA issues an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report / SR&ED Review Report assigning one of five formal eligibility determinations to each project: AW (All Work Meets), SW (Some Work Meets), NW (No Work Meets), UN (Unsubstantiated), or AAF (Accepted as Filed). If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a written Proposal Package / Proposal Letter giving the claimant 30 calendar days to submit additional rebuttal evidence or clarifications before the file is closed and a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.
8.3 Administrative Dispute Resolution, Notices of Objection, and Judicial Appeals

If a claimant disagrees with the conduct or preliminary findings of an SR&ED review, the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025) and Publication P148 (Resolving your Dispute: Objection and appeal rights under the Income Tax Act) establish a five-stage escalation hierarchy:

items: Step 1 — Assigned Reviewers (RTA / FR): Raise factual misunderstandings or submit clarifying technical/financial documentation directly to the RTA and FR during the review or within the 30-day proposal window.

Step 2 — Review Managers (RTM / FRM): If unresolved with the reviewers, escalate to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM), who review the factual record and perspectives of both parties.

Step 3 — Formal Administrative Review (AR) via Form RC532: If concerns remain unresolved after Step 2 and the claimant has received the Proposal Package, the claimant may request an Administrative Review (AR) by notifying the reviewers before the 30-day proposal period expires and submitting Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) (before the file is closed) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the AR is not a second technical review; rather, the Assistant Director adjudicates strictly whether (a) the claimant received Due Process (clear questions, reasonable time to respond, consideration of all submitted evidence, clear written reasons) and (b) the review complied with SR&ED legislation and CRA policies.

Step 4 — Notice of Objection (CRA Appeals Branch): Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has a statutory deadline of 90 calendar days from the date on the notice (or for individuals/graduated rate estates, the later of 90 days or 1 year after the T1 filing due date) to file a formal Notice of Objection online via My Business Account / Represent a Client or by mail using Form T400A / Form RC592 addressed to the Chief of Appeals at the Appeals Intake Centre. (A one-year extension of time to object may be requested if the taxpayer was unable to object or intended to object within the 90-day period). If a corporation (together with related corporations) has taxable capital employed in Canada exceeding $10,000,000 at the end of the taxation year, it is classified as a large corporation and must reasonably describe each issue in the Notice of Objection, specify the exact dollar amount of relief sought for each issue, provide the supporting facts and reasons, and pay 50% of the disputed amount upfront while awaiting the outcome of the objection or appeal.

Step 5 — Judicial Appeals to the Courts: A Notice of Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada must be received within 90 days of the date the CRA sends its decision on the objection (or anytime after 90 days have elapsed if the CRA has not issued a decision). A judgment of the Tax Court of Canada may be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal within 30 days of the final judgment (excluding July and August), and an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada must be filed within 60 days of the Federal Court of Appeal's judgment (excluding July).

body.text: 8.4 Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsection 163(2)) and Criminal Fraud Enforcement

Under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act, every person who, knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in, agrees to, or accepts the making of a false statement or omission in an initial or amended return or Form T661 is liable to a civil penalty equal to the greater of $100 and 50% of the sum of:

items: The understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a), with any reported loss deemed not less than zero under subsection 163(2.1) if non-business/personal expenses were injected into the SR&ED pool, and with overstated pool deductions and overstated non-refundable ITCs deemed deducted first before legitimate credits); plus
The entire overstated refundable SR&ED ITC claimed as a cash refund (paragraph 163(2)(d)).

body.text: Under subsection 163(3), the burden of proof rests on the CRA to establish on a balance of probabilities that the false statement resulted from knowing misconduct or gross negligence rather than simple oversight or a misunderstanding of the Act. However, the CRA's policy explicitly targets claimants who fabricate SR&ED activities, claim normal commercial costs for non-existent R&D, plagiarize technical descriptions, or repeatedly claim unsubstantiated or ineligible amounts after receiving prior written warnings from the CRA. In cases involving fabricated dates or false representations, courts have also imposed fines of 150% to 300% of the claimed credits (R. v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018; Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173).
9. Landmark Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents (1996–2026)

Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) governs every aspect of technical eligibility, evidentiary substantiation, financial calculation, and procedural compliance. The table below synthesizes the foundational and recent (up to 2026) judicial precedents across Canadian tax law:

headers: Judicial Holding & Precedential Impact on SR&ED Audits

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553
Definition of SR&ED under s. 248(1); hydraulic physical modelling

Landmark Precedent (Taxpayer Win on 4 of 5 projects): Justice Bowman established the five-criterion test for SR&ED, recognized "system uncertainty" (where known components interact unpredictably), distinguished routine engineering from technological advancement, and held that contemporaneous documentation is essential.
Evidentiary proof of testing; death of key engineer

Appellate Precedent (Taxpayer Win on Appeal): Endorsed Northwest Hydraulic at the appellate level; held that while repeatability and documented test data are required to prove systematic investigation, courts assess available evidence sympathetically where the key engineer died prior to trial.
Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen 96-4369-IT-G
Meaning of "technological advancement" when hypothesis fails
Taxpayer Win: Held that conclusively disproving or rejecting a scientific or technological hypothesis is itself a technological advancement.
Mandatory nature of the five Northwest Hydraulic questions
Crown Win: Confirmed that the five criteria articulated in Northwest Hydraulic are settled appellate law for interpreting s. 248(1).
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355
Routine engineering vs. experimental development in manufacturing
Crown Win: Upheld disallowance of manufacturing overhaul projects where problems were solved without satisfying the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen 2014 TCC 313
Sparse written documentation; impartiality of CRA expert witness

Taxpayer Win: Justice Jorré ruled that highly credible oral testimony can counter sparse written records, and found that a CRA employee acting as an expert witness was not sufficiently impartial where he confused internal CRA administrative policy with his duty to the court.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen 2015 TCC 77
Post-sale printer design uncertainties & proving project filing

Taxpayer Win: Confirmed that resolving genuine technological uncertainties arising after commercial sale qualifies as SR&ED, and accepted credible oral evidence proving a project narrative was filed with the claim.
Easyway Cattle Co. Ltd. v. The Queen 2015 TCC 211 & Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen 2017 TCC 9
Strict enforcement of the 18-month SR&ED filing deadline
Crown Wins: Held that the 18-month deadline is absolute; failing to file Schedule T2SCH31 on time (Easyway Cattle) or relying on projects filed only by a related company (Westsource) bars the claim.
Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen 2019 TCC 32 & Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen 2019 TCC 11
Estimated SR&ED hours; company know-how vs. general technological advancement

Crown Wins: In Concept Danat, the Court held that simply estimated hours without substantiating or contemporaneous evidence are not acceptable; in Dock Edge +, the Court held that advancing only internal company knowledge (with only 3 pages of notes and a few photos) does not advance general technological understanding.
CRL Engineering Ltd. v. The Queen 2019 TCC 65

Taxpayer Win: Allowed software SR&ED claim where the taxpayer's expert witness demonstrated that weekly system repository snapshots and an active project wiki logged data, methods, issues, and results contemporaneously.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada 2021 FCA 88 & National R&D Inc. v. Canada 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72
Cumulative nature of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria in metalwork and SQL software

Crown Wins: The Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed that each of the questions in the five-factor Northwest Hydraulic test must be answered in the affirmative; merely having hypotheses accepted (National R&D) without convincing the Court on the remaining criteria fails.
Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King 2023 TCC 18
System uncertainty in complex mechanical/tractor integration
Taxpayer Win: Demonstrated how illustrating system integration issues establishes valid system uncertainties.
Cloud SaaS integration & open-source framework (React/Redux) performance

Landmark Software Taxpayer Win: Held that resolving systemic uncertainty in open-source tool integration (React/Redux) went beyond routine debugging/optimization and satisfied the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) & Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 183)

Crown Wins: Dismissed claims where engineering work consisted of trial-and-error prototyping with vague hypotheses (Vortex) or where 13 food-processing projects lacked proven technological uncertainty and systematic records and relied on wages estimated and split evenly across batches (Tuna Temple).
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King 2025 TCC 173
Plagiarized technical narratives, statute-barred years, and s. 163(2) penalties

Split Decision (Critical Compliance Warning): While allowing certain 2007–2008 heating-element projects, the Court held that plagiarized supplier/website text in technical reports constituted a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported s. 163(2) penalties.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King 2026 TCC 7
Industrial control software: SIL 4 train control vs. SCADA modernization

2026 Split Decision: Allowed the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control project on cumulative system uncertainty, but upheld the disallowance of $1,293,692 for the SCADACOM-5 project, ruling that modernization and scale-up using known tools is product development, not experimental development.

body.text: 10. Comprehensive Audit Readiness Checklist for Canadian Claimants

To ensure full statutory compliance and audit defensibility under the post-Bill C-15 regime, Canadian corporations and their tax advisors should execute the following ten-point verification protocol during every taxation year:

items: Evaluate Pre-Claim Approval Eligibility Before Project Kickoff: If the corporation (or partnership) has gross business income under $25,000,000 and is in good standing with the CRA, submit an optional Pre-Claim Approval application via My Business Account before starting new SR&ED projects to obtain an 8-week up-front technical determination and qualify for the accelerated 90-day post-filing review standard.

Model the CCPC Revenue Election vs. Taxable Capital Phase-Out: For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, verify whether the CCPC's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000; if so, model the subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) election to compute the $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the three-year average gross revenue test ($15M–$75M) applicable to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).

Assess Public Company Eligibility Under the New ECPC Rules: For Canadian public corporations not controlled by non-residents, confirm qualification as an ECPC under subsection 127(9) to claim the enhanced 35% refundable federal ITC (and the 10% refundable BC SR&ED credit, where applicable) on up to $6,000,000 of expenditures.

Substantiate Capital Intent and Operating Time Logs Post-December 15, 2024: For all servers, GPUs, testing rigs, and lab equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, document ASA (≥90%) lifetime SR&ED intent in capital budgets and purchase memos at acquisition (Line 390), and maintain contemporaneous equipment usage logbooks tracking operating hours by project to substantiate Lines 262–263 or First-Term / Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE >50%) on Line 504 and Part 6C.

Model the Irrevocable Traditional vs. Proxy Method Election: Prior to filing Form T661, compare the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 160 against actual incremental overhead, non-ASA equipment lease costs, and metered cloud computing/software tool expenses claimable under the Traditional Method on Line 162 / Line 360—remembering that the election is irrevocable once filed (subsection 37(10)).

Enforce Contemporaneous Time Tracking and Specified Employee Caps: Eliminate retrospective percentage estimates (Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32; Tuna Temple, 2025 TCC 183), strip all bonuses and profit-based remuneration from specified employees (subsection 37(9)), apply the 5 × YMPE direct wage cap ($356,500 in 2025; $373,000 in 2026) and the lesser of 75% or 2.5 × YMPE proxy base cap ($178,250 in 2025; $186,500 in 2026), and pay all accrued bonuses and wages within 180 days of year-end (subsection 78(4)).

Structure Subcontractor and Non-Arm's Length Agreements: Ensure arm's length SR&ED contracts specify work performed in Canada by a taxable supplier and obtain annual written capital look-through confirmations within 90 days of calendar year-end (subsection 37(15)); for non-arm's length R&D performers, execute Form T1146 under subsection 127(13) to transfer qualified expenditures to the payer.

Optimize Provincial Credits and Renunciations: In Ontario, confirm the treatment of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures for Schedule 566 (8% OITC) and Schedule 508 (3.5% ORDTC), given that the Ontario Ministry of Finance's OITC page still states that capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 are not qualified expenditures, and evaluate waiving the non-refundable ORDTC within 6 months of year-end if in a prolonged tax-loss position. In Québec, transition taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 to Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (CRIC), capturing both R&D (Code 112) and eligible regulatory/design pre-commercialization activities (Code 113) as well as capital property acquisition costs above the employee-indexed exclusion threshold.

Draft Original, Evidence-Backed Technical Narratives (Lines 242, 244, 246): Adhere strictly to the 350 / 700 / 350 word limits, select the accurate 5-digit Statistics Canada CRDC code (RDF#####) on Line 207, link every narrative to dated repository commits, test logs, and wiki snapshots (CRL Engineering, 2019 TCC 65), and never copy supplier or website text (Tempora, 2025 TCC 173).

File Ahead of the 18-Month Statutory Bar and Verify Part 9 Disclosures: Submit Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, and all provincial schedules at least 90 days before the non-waivable 18-month reporting deadline (subsection 220(2.2)), and verify complete accuracy of Part 9 Claim Preparer Information to prevent the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty.
